# Research question

**To what extent does the reduction in households' direct out-of-pocket health expenditure influence individual health behaviours, and to what extent can it foster the emergence of moral hazard?**

In most developed countries, health care is largely financed through public spending or collective insurance. The expected effect is positive: when access to care no longer depends on income, prevention, screening and treatment improve, and life expectancy rises. By contrast, countries where out-of-pocket spending (the share paid directly by the patient) is high experience more forgone care and greater health inequalities. A first part of our work is therefore to check whether a lower out-of-pocket share is associated with a higher life expectancy.

Moral hazard is a key concept in health economics : it is defined as the phenomenon where individuals, when **insured against health care costs**, may engage in **riskier behavior** (*ex-ante* moral hazard) or **overconsume** health care resources (*ex-post* moral hazard) because they do not bear the full financial responsibility for those costs. This can lead to market inefficiency and an overallocation of health care services.

In this project, we’ll try to assess whether the concept of ex-ante moral hazard is a real and measurable phenomenon, or rather a theoretical risk whose magnitude remains limited compared with the benefits of a well-funded health system. */!if the project is not long enough, we’ll try to assess the concept of ex-post moral hazard as well.*

We can state two working hypotheses:

- **H1.** A lower out-of-pocket share is associated with a higher life expectancy, even after controlling for GDP per capita.
- **H2.** A lower out-of-pocket share is associated with higher alcohol consumption and tobacco use (moral hazard), but the effect is small compared with the gain in life expectancy.

Methodologically, we will carry out a longitudinal study. Since the studies are conducted at the country level and there are not enough countries in the world to reach 1000 units, we use data by year: each observation is a country in a given year. This gives a panel of several thousand observations and allows us to follow the same country over time, for instance with country fixed effects, to compare a country with itself rather than with very different countries.

**LIMIT**The main limitation of the project is that we only have national averages. A relation observed between countries does not necessarily hold for individuals (ecological fallacy), so we cannot draw firm conclusions about individual behaviours. Our results will describe associations and not proven causal effects.

# Data sources

## Links and how to reproduce the data selection

MOST files are downloaded from the World Bank Open Data portal. The World Bank only redistributes the health and behaviour indicators, which are produced by the WHO. To reproduce the selection (downlaod as csv files):

| DATA | Producer | Indicator page | Local file |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Out-of-pocket health expenditure (% of current health expenditure) | WHO GHED, via World Bank | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.XPD.OOPC.CH.ZS?downloadformat=csv> | `data/out_of_pocket` |
| Alcohol consumption per capita (litres of pure alcohol, 15+) | WHO GHO, via World Bank | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.ALC.PCAP.LI?downloadformat=csv> | `data/alcohol` |
| Tobacco use (smoking prevalence) | WHO GHO, via World Bank | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.PRV.SMOK?downloadformat=csv> | `data/tobacco.csv` |
| GDP per capita, PPP (constant international \$) | World Bank (ICP / WDI) | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD?downloadformat=csv> | `data/gdp_ppp` |
| Life expectancy at birth, total (years) | World Bank (WDI) | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.LE00.IN?downloadformat=csv> | `data/life_expectancy` |
| Mortality caused by road traffic injury (per 100.000 person) | World Health Organization (WHO) | <https://api.worldbank.org/v2/en/indicator/SH.STA.TRAF.P5?downloadformat=csv> | `data/mortality_car.csv` |
| Educational attainment, at least Bachelor's or equivalent, population 25+, total (%) | UNESCO | \<\> | `data/.csv` |

## Short description of the sources and cleaning

Our data come mainly from datasets of the World Health Organization (WHO) that are redistributed by the World Bank. The point of this part is mainly to make the dataset proper to a longitudinal analysis.

```{r}
#|include: false

#usually, Word bank files contains 4 lines that are useless.
# we can check it the following way 

readLines("Data/alcohol/API_SH.ALC.PCAP.LI_DS2_en_csv_v2_3878.csv", n = 6)
readLines("Data/health_expenditure/API_SH.XPD.CHEX.GD.ZS_DS2_en_csv_v2_73563.csv", n = 6)
readLines("Data/gdp_ppp/API_NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD_DS2_en_csv_v2_1629.csv", n = 6)
readLines("Data/life_expectancy/API_SP.DYN.LE00.IN_DS2_en_csv_v2_1528.csv", n = 6)

```

## Most important variables /!!!!!!\\ à reprendre faut faire plus long

| Variable | Description |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `country`, `iso3` | unique identification code of the country. They are the first key used to join the files. |
| `year` | Calendar year of the observation. |
| `life_exp` | Life expectancy at birth in years. |
| `oop_share` | Out-of-pocket expenditure as a percentage of current health expenditure. High values mean a weak financial protection. Main explanatory variable. |
| `alcohol` | Alcohol consumption per capita (litres of pure alcohol, population 15+, recorded and unrecorded). Proxy of risky behaviour. |
| `tobacco` | Prevalence of tobacco smoking. Proxy of risky behaviour. |
| `gdp_pc` | GDP per capita in PPP, constant international dollars. Control variable for the level of wealth. |

### World Bank files (WDI)

Five of our files come from the World Development Indicators (WDI) database of the World Bank. Each indicator was downloaded as a CSV from the World Bank Data website. The files for alcohol, GDP and life expectancy were last updated on 2026-10-08, the files for health expenditure and road mortality on 2026-11-11.

- **Alcohol consumption** (`SH.ALC.PCAP.LI`): total alcohol consumption per capita, in litres of pure alcohol, for people aged 15 and over, adjusted of the tourist consumtion. These are **projected estimates** produced by the WHO, not direct national measurements.According to the file `Metadata_Country_API_SH.ALC.PCAP.LI_DS2_en_csv_v2_3878`, the world bank takes into account, when there are, the two exanges rates.
- **Current Governmental health expenditure** (`SH.XPD.CHEX.GD.ZS`): total health spending as a percentage of GDP, from the WHO Global Health Expenditure Database.Estimates of current health expenditures include healthcare goods and services consumed during each year. This indicator **does not include capital** health expenditures such as buildings, machinery, IT and stocks of vaccines for emergency or outbreaks, according to the metadatas : 
- **GDP per capita** (`NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD`): GDP per capita at **purchasing power parity**, in constant 2021 international dollars.
- **Life expectancy** (`SP.DYN.LE00.IN`): life expectancy at birth, total, in years. It "indicates the number of years a newborn infant would live if prevailing patterns of mortality at the time of its birth were to stay the same throughout its life.", note: Derived from male and female life expectancy at birth from sources such as Eurostat: Demographic Statistics.,

- **Road traffic mortality** (`SH.STA.TRAF.P5`): deaths caused by road traffic injury, per 100,000 population.

### Cleaning steps for the World Bank files

All five files have the same structure, so one function cleans them all:

1.  The first 4 lines are a presentation header (source, update date), so we skip them.
2.  Each line ends with an extra comma, which creates an empty unnamed column. We drop it.
3.  The files are in *wide* format (one column per year, 1960 to 2025). We reshape them to *long* format (one row per country and year).
4.  Years without a value are removed, since many indicators only cover part of the period.
5.  The files mix countries and aggregates (World, Euro area, income groups...). We keep only real countries, using the country metadata file: aggregates have no `Region`.

```{r}
#| label: wb-cleaning

# country metadata: aggregates have an empty Region
meta_file <- list.files(here("Data", "alcohol"),
                        pattern = "^Metadata_Country", full.names = TRUE)
countries <- vroom(meta_file, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(!is.na(Region)) |>
  select(iso3 = `Country Code`, region = Region, income_group = IncomeGroup)

# to go faster, Claude created a function read_wb that takes ... for argument & uses tidyr for cleaning the world bank databases 
read_wb <- function(path, value_name) {
  vroom(path, skip = 4, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(-starts_with("...")) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = matches("^[0-9]{4}$"),
      names_to = "year",
      values_to = value_name,
      names_transform = as.integer,
      values_transform = as.numeric,
      values_drop_na = TRUE
    ) |>
    semi_join(countries, by = c("Country Code" = "iso3")) |>
    select(country = `Country Name`, iso3 = `Country Code`,
           year, all_of(value_name))
}

alcohol <- read_wb(
  here("Data", "alcohol", "API_SH.ALC.PCAP.LI_DS2_en_csv_v2_3878.csv"),
  "alcohol_litres")
pub_health_exp <- read_wb(
  here("Data", "health_expenditure", "API_SH.XPD.CHEX.GD.ZS_DS2_en_csv_v2_73563.csv"),
  "health_exp_gdp")
out_pocket <- read_wb(
  here("Data", "out_of_pocket", "API_SH.XPD.OOPC.CH.ZS_DS2_en_csv_v2_62345.csv"),
  "oop_share")
gdp <- read_wb(
  here("Data", "gdp_ppp", "API_NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD_DS2_en_csv_v2_1629.csv"),
  "gdp_pc_ppp")
life_exp <- read_wb(
  here("Data", "life_expectancy", "API_SP.DYN.LE00.IN_DS2_en_csv_v2_1528.csv"),
  "life_expectancy")
road_deaths <- read_wb(
  here("Data", "death_trafic_injury", "API_SH.STA.TRAF.P5_DS2_en_csv_v2_72972.csv"),
  "road_deaths_100k")
tobacco <- read_wb(
  here("Data", "tobacco",
       "API_SH.PRV.SMOK_DS2_en_csv_v2.csv"),
  "tobacco"
)
```

After cleaning, here is what each indicator covers:

```{r}
#| label: wb-coverage
list(alcohol = alcohol, health_exp = health_exp, gdp = gdp,
     life_exp = life_exp, road_deaths = road_deaths) |>
  imap(\(d, name) tibble(
    indicator    = name,
    countries    = n_distinct(d$iso3),
    first_year   = min(d$year),
    last_year    = max(d$year),
    observations = nrow(d)
  )) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  knitr::kable()
```


# Tables 

```{r}
data.frame(
  Dataset = c("Alcohol", "GDP", "Life expectancy",
              "Health expenditure", "Road mortality"),
  Rows = c(nrow(alcohol), nrow(gdp), nrow(life_exp),
           nrow(health_exp), nrow(road_deaths)),
  Columns = c(ncol(alcohol), ncol(gdp), ncol(life_exp),
              ncol(health_exp), ncol(road_deaths))
) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

# PLOT OF THE MAIN VARIABLE 


```{r}
library(ggplot2)

life_exp |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    mean_life_exp = mean(
      life_expectancy,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_life_exp)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Evolution of global life expectancy",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Life expectancy (years)"
  ) 
```

More interesting : life expectancy according to out of pocket expenditure : 

```{r}
#need to join the two datasets first 

panel <- life_exp |>
  left_join(out_pocket, by = c("iso3", "year"))

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(panel, aes(x = oop_share, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Life expectancy according to out-of-pocket expenditure",
    subtitle = "Relationship between health expenditure and life expectancy",
    x = "Out-of-pocket expenditure (% of current health expenditure)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
